claims.text: Small additions of chromium enhance the corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
Chromium additions promote in situ formation of a thin Cr-rich passive oxide layer.
The Cr-rich passive oxide layer is adherent and uniform.
The Cr-rich passive oxide layer inhibits localized pitting and general corrosion.
Controlled oxidizing heat treatment and subsequent service-environment exposure promote passive-film formation.
The structural mediator is a continuous, adherent Cr-rich oxide film on the steel surface.
Chromium in the alloy oxidizes preferentially.
Preferential chromium oxidation forms a stable passive layer.
The passive layer retards iron dissolution.
The passive layer inhibits the initiation and propagation of corrosion sites.
Under identical exposure conditions, higher-chromium steels will have a significantly lower corrosion rate than lower-chromium steels.
Higher-chromium steels will exhibit less weight loss and less pitting than the baseline steels.
Surface analysis of higher-chromium steels will reveal a distinct Cr-rich passive film.
Lower-chromium or untreated baseline samples that fail to form a robust passive film will exhibit greater corrosion and more severe localized attack.
The proposed mechanism should apply in moderate-chloride, standard-temperature, and relevant radiation environments while the passive layer remains stable.
A statistically insignificant corrosion-rate difference, absence of a measurable Cr-rich film, or similar protection in the baseline would falsify the proposed mechanism.
